To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

simultaneous remote sensing observations can be used to verify emission inventories, and can distinguish emissions from different sources, including power plants and urban emissions, with different emission factors.
we demonstrate the feasibility of remote sensing observations of atmospheric CO2, CO and NO2 to verify and attribute emissions from power plants.

we have demonstrated the first simultaneous remote sensing measurements of column abundances and isotopes of CO2, and co-emitted pollutants (CO, CO2, and NO2), in the Four Corners region of the U.S., and have used the measurements to verify and attribute emissions from fossil fuel power plants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the verification of emissions of CO2, SO2 and NOx from large point sources.
the ability of remote sensing to verify emissions and emission reduction technologies.
developing a new methodology for the remote sensing of atmospheric CO2 emissions from anthropogenic sources and the attribution of the sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the simultaneous observations of CO2 (and δ13CO2), NO2, and SO2 from space and ground can be used to verify and attribute emissions of CO2, and NO2 from power plants and other sources in a region with multiple sources.
we demonstrate the feasibility of remote sensing observations to identify emissions from individual power plants and to verify emissions from power plants.

we can now measure CO2 and co-emitted pollutants (NO2, CO) from ground and space, and that we can verify emission reductions from power plants, and that we are now able to distinguish between different sources of CO2, such as clean and dirty power plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the remote sensing of CO2 and NOy can be used to verify emissions from power plants.
the remote sensing observations of atmospheric column enhancements in CO and NO2, and the δ13CO2 isotopic ratio, can be used to identify and quantify the emissions from large power plants.
the simultaneous remote sensing observations are able to distinguish the emission factors and abate technologies from ground and satellite.
The main takeaway from our work is that
remote sensing of CO2, δ13CO2, CO, NO2, SO, and O3 can be used in tandem to inform, attribute, and verify emission inventies.
the simultaneous remote sensing observations can provide a unique, high-frequency, and cost-effective means to verify emissions from power plants.
the simultaneous remote sensing of CO2 and pollutants can be used for emission verification and to identify sources of emissions with distinct emission factors.
